cases.case_name: Kaho'ohanohano ex rel. Morales-Kaho'ohanohano v. Department of Human Services
cases.holding: The court affirmed a negligence judgment against DHS, holding that once DHS receives a report of suspected child abuse, HRS chapter 587 and its implementing rules create a special relationship and an affirmative legal duty to investigate reasonably and to protect the reported child from further harm.
cases.quote: Accordingly, we conclude that DHS had a duty to protect Minor under the circumstances of this case.

relevance.INP-01: This is the controlling Hawai'i authority that a mandated report triggers a legally enforceable DHS duty, so a mandatory reporter's report is not merely informational but starts a duty-bearing process.
relevance.INP-02: A report from any source, once received, creates the same special relationship and protective duty, so third-party reports carry the same downstream legal consequence.
relevance.INP-03: The abuse report here came to DHS from the Maui Police Department, confirming that a law-enforcement referral triggers DHS's investigative and protective duty.
relevance.INP-06: A hotline or telephoned report received by DHS starts the statutory duty to investigate competently; anonymity of the source does not excuse the agency's obligation.
relevance.INP-07: Medical findings reported to DHS trigger the duty to conduct a reasonable and competent investigation before returning a child to a suspected abuser.
relevance.INP-08: Although the report here was not from a school, the duty the court recognized attaches on receipt of any statutory report, including educator reports.
relevance.INP-09: The decision supplies the accountability backstop when systemic oversight reveals inadequate CPS investigation: Hawai'i permits money-damages liability against DHS.
relevance.INP-10: The court measured DHS's escalation from intake to investigation against an ordinary negligence standard, not a deferential professional-judgment standard.
relevance.DEC-01: Screening out or minimally reviewing a report does not discharge DHS's duty; an unreasonable investigation after a report is actionable negligence.
relevance.DEC-02: The decision defines the standard of care governing the acceptance and conduct of an investigation in Hawai'i.
relevance.ACT-06: DHS's duty encompassed obtaining protective action for a child already medically documented as injured, informing decisions to secure emergency care.
relevance.OUT-06: This is Hawai'i's leading case on agency liability where a child suffers catastrophic injury after a report to DHS.
relevance.FAIL-04: It establishes that serious harm to a child under agency attention after a report can result in State tort liability, including negligent infliction of emotional distress to family members.
relevance.PMC-01: Performance failures in investigation quality that federal reviews measure are, in Hawai'i, also independently actionable in tort.
relevance.PMC-04: The factual record the court reviewed is the template for what a fatality or near-fatality review must examine: report intake, investigation quality, and return-home decisions.

cases.holding: The court held that under article I, section 5 of the Hawai'i Constitution indigent parents have a right to court-appointed counsel in termination proceedings, and that the family court abused its discretion by not appointing counsel until nineteen months after DHS petitioned for temporary foster custody.
cases.quote: indigent parents are guaranteed the right to court-appointed counsel in termination proceedings

relevance.DEC-05: Filing the petition is the point at which the indigent parent's right to appointed counsel attaches, so the petition decision has immediate due-process consequences.
relevance.OUT-01: Counsel from the outset is what allows a parent to engage the service plan and pursue reunification before permanency deadlines run.
relevance.OUT-02: This is the Hawai'i constitutional foundation for the right to counsel in any proceeding that may end in termination of parental rights.

cases.holding: The court held that where the right to counsel applies in a termination case it includes the right to effective counsel and that an HFCR Rule 60(b)(6) motion is an appropriate vehicle for such a claim, but affirmed the denial of relief on this record given the delay's harm to the child.
cases.quote: the right to counsel in termination of parental rights cases, where applicable, includes the right to effective counsel

relevance.OUT-02: It supplies the ineffective-assistance standard and the procedural vehicle for attacking a termination order after the fact.
relevance.FAIL-01: It defines when a court may and may not undo its own termination order for counsel failures, and stresses the countervailing weight of the child's need for permanency.

cases.holding: The court held that incarceration does not itself forfeit parental rights but may be weighed in the safe-family-home analysis, and separately that alleged ADA violations are not a defense to a termination proceeding; it affirmed termination after finding DHS made reasonable efforts.
cases.quote: a criminal charge, conviction, or incarceration does not per se result in the forfeiture of parental rights, but confinement can be considered a factor

relevance.ACT-02: It frames how a service plan must be assessed for an incarcerated or otherwise disabled parent rather than treating status as dispositive.
relevance.OUT-01: The same opinion holds DHS made reasonable efforts to reunify under the circumstances, illustrating the reunification-efforts inquiry for a confined parent.
relevance.FAIL-05: It bars status-based forfeiture of parental rights and (in the companion holding) rules that ADA violations must be litigated separately rather than as a termination defense.

cases.holding: The court held that DHS as permanent custodian has discretion in the first instance to select a child's permanent placement, that the party challenging the recommendation bears a preponderance burden, and that neither HRS chapter 587A nor Title IV-E imposes a mandatory relative-placement preference for permanent placement.
cases.quote: the party challenging DHS's permanent placement recommendation bears the burden of proving by a preponderance of the evidence that the permanent placement is not in the child's best interests

relevance.ACT-03: It sets the allocation of decisional authority and the burden of proof whenever a foster placement is contested in Hawai'i family court.
relevance.ACT-04: The court expressly rejected the argument that state or federal law compels a relative placement preference at the permanent-placement stage.
relevance.OUT-03: Permanency through a relative or kin caregiver must be shown to be in the child's best interests by the challenging party, not presumed.
relevance.FAIL-03: The court analyzed and rejected the claim that Title IV-E conditions federal funds on relative placement, narrowing the federal-compliance theory available to litigants.
relevance.PMC-01: It is the Hawai'i decision that construes the federal IV-E placement provisions that federal reviews measure states against.

cases.holding: The court held that a hānai relative who is the child's resource caregiver has an interest sufficient to intervene as of right under HFCR Rule 24(a)(2) in a child welfare case, and that the family court must weigh the child's hānai relationships in the best-interests analysis.
cases.quote: we conclude that, when conducting a best interest of the child analysis, family courts must consider that child’s hānai relationships

relevance.INP-05: A hānai caregiver who steps forward on the child's behalf has a recognized legal footing to be heard rather than being treated as a stranger to the case.
relevance.ACT-04: Hawai'i's kinship analysis reaches beyond blood relation to the culturally recognized hānai relationship.
relevance.OUT-03: Permanency planning must account for hānai bonds, which can support guardianship or adoption by a non-blood kin caregiver.
relevance.FAIL-05: Disregarding a Native Hawaiian hānai relationship in placement decisions is legal error, not merely a cultural preference.

cases.holding: The court held that termination under HRS § 587A-33 requires a finding that the proposed permanent plan is in the child's best interests, and that the ICA erred by substituting the more general family court provision, HRS § 571-61(b)(1)(E), to avoid that requirement.
cases.quote: the family court erred in terminating Father’s parental rights under HRS § 587A-33, the CPA Provision, without finding that DHS’s proposed permanent plan was in KK’s best interests

relevance.DEC-03: It identifies the specific statutory criteria, including the service-plan and safe-family-home elements, that must be proven by clear and convincing evidence before rights can be ended.
relevance.ACT-02: The safe-family-home analysis is expressly tied to whether the parent can parent safely even with the assistance of a service plan.
relevance.OUT-01: The two-year outer limit for foreseeable reunification is part of the same statutory provision the court enforced.
relevance.OUT-02: Termination cannot rest on the general family court statute where the Child Protective Act adds a permanent-plan best-interests element.
relevance.OUT-05: Where the permanent plan is not in the child's best interests, the CPA termination petition fails on its own terms.
relevance.FAIL-01: This is a Hawai'i Supreme Court reversal of an appellate court for circumventing a statutory element of termination.

cases.holding: The court held that counsel must be appointed for an indigent parent when DHS files a petition for family supervision, not merely when it seeks foster custody, and that failure to do so is structural error requiring vacatur of the foster-custody and termination orders.
cases.quote: The family court's failure to appoint Mother counsel when DHS filed its petition for family supervision was structural error and cannot be deemed harmless.

relevance.DEC-05: The filing of any petition that can lead to custody or termination, including a family supervision petition, triggers the appointment duty.
relevance.DEC-06: Choosing a lesser, non-removal court track does not lower the parent's right to counsel, because foster custody or termination remains possible.
relevance.FAIL-01: Structural error of this kind requires vacatur without harmless-error analysis, making it a primary ground for reversing agency-obtained orders.

cases.holding: The court reaffirmed that counsel must be appointed at the onset of a parental rights case, but held that a later break in representation caused by the parent's own voluntary absence is not structural error so long as the proceeding remains fundamentally fair.
cases.quote: A family court must timely appoint counsel in parental rights cases.

relevance.INP-03: The opinion sets out HRS § 587A-8, under which a police officer assumes protective custody without a court order when a child faces imminent harm, and the transfer of that custody to DHS.
relevance.INP-07: The case arose from a hospital NICU referral after the newborn tested positive for unprescribed opiates, the paradigm medical-disclosure entry point.
relevance.INP-12: It quotes and applies the statutory grounds for warrantless police protective custody and the department's assumption of temporary foster custody.
relevance.DEC-04: The statutory imminent-harm and flight-risk criteria for taking a child without a court order are set out verbatim in the opinion.
relevance.ACT-03: It traces the path from police protective custody to DHS temporary foster custody and the petition that follows.

cases.case_name: In re Guardianship of I.W. and T.E.
cases.holding: The court held that the presumption that a fit parent acts in the child's best interest survives the parent's consent to a guardianship, and that article I, sections 5 and 6 of the Hawai'i Constitution require clear and convincing evidence of unfitness before that presumption may be set aside.
cases.quote: the rebuttable presumption that a fit parent acts in the best interest of their child extends to guardianship proceedings

relevance.INP-05: A parent who voluntarily asks for help by consenting to a guardianship does not thereby waive the constitutional presumption in their favor.
relevance.ACT-01: Consent to a voluntary arrangement is not a waiver of parental rights, which constrains how agencies may use voluntary placements.
relevance.OUT-03: This is the current Hawai'i standard governing guardianship as a permanency outcome: clear and convincing evidence of unfitness, with best interests judged by a preponderance.

cases.holding: The court reversed the ICA and held that the Child Protective Act is not constitutionally infirm, because its criteria do not allow termination absent clear and convincing evidence bearing on the individual parent's unfitness, and affirmed the termination order.
cases.quote: it does not permit the termination of parental rights in the absence of clear and convincing evidence that a parent is "unfit"

relevance.DEC-03: It is the leading Hawai'i statement that a founded case must ultimately be proved to the clear and convincing standard as to the individual parent, not the household generally.
relevance.OUT-02: This is the Hawai'i Supreme Court's due-process validation of the CPA termination criteria under both constitutions.
relevance.OUT-05: If the evidence does not meet the clear and convincing standard as to the parent, the petition must fail.

cases.holding: The court vacated the permanent custody order and remanded, holding that the family court abused its discretion by reappointing a guardian ad litem for the mother without the hearing HRS § 587-34(d) requires and that she was thereby deprived of a fair hearing.
cases.quote: Mother was deprived of her parental rights without a fair hearing

relevance.FAIL-01: It is a direct Hawai'i Supreme Court vacatur of a permanent custody order for procedural error in the conduct of the hearing.

cases.holding: The court held that the family court may exercise chapter 587 protective powers whenever it has the necessary information, regardless of whether the case began under chapter 571 or on a formal chapter 587 petition, but reversed the portion of the order requiring DHS foster board payments after the minor turned eighteen.
cases.quote: we reverse those orders that require the DHS to pay foster board payments for periods after the Minor's eighteenth birthday

relevance.INP-04: It confirms that a judge who learns of possible abuse in another proceeding may invoke chapter 587 protective authority directly.
relevance.ACT-01: The family court's flexible chapter 587 authority underpins service and supervision arrangements short of removal.
relevance.ACT-05: It confirms the breadth of the family court's protective powers to fashion orders addressing a child's safety.
relevance.DEC-06: Protective action may proceed without a formal abuse petition where the court has the necessary information.
relevance.OUT-04: This is the Hawai'i authority limiting DHS foster board payments past the youth's eighteenth birthday absent a justification in the record.

cases.holding: The court held that the family court lacked jurisdiction to order the Department of Health to fund services where IDEA remedies were unexhausted, but that the child's status as a ward of the State created an independent state-law basis obligating the State, with DHS ultimately accountable, to pay for his mental health services.
cases.quote: we hold that the family court correctly concluded that an independent state basis exists under which John is entitled to receive payment for the mental health services

relevance.INP-05: Foster families who seek help for a child in their care have a state-law route to funded services independent of federal education law.
relevance.ACT-01: Voluntary service arrangements for a State ward carry a state funding obligation that DHS cannot disclaim.
relevance.ACT-06: It is the Hawai'i authority obligating the State to pay for a ward's psychological and mental health care.
relevance.OUT-04: The State's obligation to fund a ward's care shapes what transitional supports a youth can demand as the case moves toward exit.

cases.holding: The court held that the family court erred by refusing to analyze the father's motion to intervene in the Child Protective Act case under HFCR Rule 24 merely because his default had not been set aside, and vacated in part for that analysis to be performed.
cases.quote: Thus, the family court should have analyzed Father's Motion to Intervene under HFCR Rule 24.

relevance.INP-04: A parent who surfaces after a case has opened must be given the Rule 24 analysis rather than being excluded by an unvacated default.

cases.court: Intermediate Court of Appeals of Hawai'i
cases.holding: The ICA held that on a contested placement the family court may not simply review DHS's placement decision for clear error but must make its own determination whether the placement serves the child's best interest, while rejecting the argument that disagreement with DHS requires removing it as custodian.
cases.quote: We conclude that the family court, based on the evidence presented, must make its own determination regarding whether the placement of the child is in the child's best interest.

relevance.ACT-03: It fixes the family court's independent role in reviewing a contested foster placement rather than deferring to the agency's finding.
relevance.ACT-04: A relative or kin caregiver contesting placement is entitled to the court's own best-interest determination on the evidence.
relevance.FAIL-01: It identifies the standard of review error that most often supports reversal of an agency placement decision in Hawai'i.

cases.court: Intermediate Court of Appeals of Hawai'i
cases.holding: The ICA affirmed an order of family supervision, holding that a chapter 587 petition is verified by a declaration under penalty of perjury, that threatened harm alone suffices to sustain the petition, and that DHS's disclosure of case information to the police was not a ground for dismissal absent particularized objection.
cases.quote: Thus, allegations of actual harm are not required to sustain a petition for family supervision and allegations of threatened harm would suffice.

relevance.INP-01: It confirms that a report describing risk rather than completed injury is legally sufficient to start and sustain protective proceedings.
relevance.INP-02: Reports of threatened harm from any source can support court intervention without proof of an accomplished injury.
relevance.INP-03: The opinion addresses and upholds DHS's sharing of case information with police, prosecutors and victim-witness counselors under the governing statutes and rules.
relevance.INP-04: It describes the verified-petition mechanics a court must find satisfied before protective jurisdiction attaches.
relevance.INP-06: A hotline-sourced allegation of threatened harm is a sufficient legal predicate for a family supervision petition.
relevance.INP-08: A disclosure by one child that establishes threatened harm to a sibling can support a petition as to that sibling.
relevance.INP-10: It shows what the escalation from report to petition must contain: threatened harm pleaded with supporting detail.
relevance.DEC-01: Screening a report out for lack of actual injury misapplies the standard, since threatened harm suffices.
relevance.DEC-03: Threatened harm is an independently sufficient founded basis under the Child Protective Act.
relevance.DEC-05: It sets the verification and pleading requirements for the petition that opens a Hawai'i dependency case.
relevance.DEC-06: Family supervision without removal is the relief the petition sought and obtained on a threatened-harm showing.
relevance.ACT-05: Court-ordered family supervision is available as a protective measure short of removing the child.
relevance.OUT-05: Conversely, where neither harm nor threatened harm is properly alleged or proven, the petition cannot stand.

cases.court: Intermediate Court of Appeals of Hawai'i
cases.holding: The ICA rejected a Native Hawaiian father's claim that ICWA's beyond-a-reasonable-doubt standard and qualified-expert requirement applied to him, holding that ICWA reaches only proceedings involving an 'Indian child' and does not include Native Hawaiians, and affirmed termination under the ordinary clear and convincing standard.
cases.quote: The ICWA clearly does not include Native Hawaiians within its purview and applies only to state-child-protective proceedings involving an "Indian child."

relevance.INP-11: This is the controlling Hawai'i holding that Native Hawaiian ancestry does not trigger ICWA, which is the single most misunderstood jurisdictional point in Hawai'i child welfare practice.

cases.court: Intermediate Court of Appeals of Hawai'i
cases.holding: On competing adoption petitions for children in DHS permanent custody, the ICA held that family courts must separately determine whether the statutory consent requirement of HRS § 578-2 is met, and that the party contending DHS unreasonably withheld consent bears a preponderance burden.
cases.quote: we hold that the party challenging DHS's action bears the burden of proving, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the withholding of consent is unreasonable

relevance.OUT-02: It governs the consent element in a contested adoption following termination of parental rights.
relevance.OUT-03: Foster or kin caregivers seeking permanency by adoption must carry the burden of showing DHS's refusal of consent was unreasonable.

cases.court: Intermediate Court of Appeals of Hawai'i
cases.holding: The ICA held that appointed counsel for an indigent parent is essential throughout proceedings that could result in termination, so that a lapse in representation during the case, and not only at its start, is constitutionally significant.
cases.quote: we hold that such an attorney is essential throughout proceedings that could result in the termination of parental rights

relevance.ACT-02: A parent must have counsel while the service plan is being imposed and enforced, not only at the termination trial.
relevance.OUT-01: Continuous representation is what allows a parent to contest compliance findings that otherwise foreclose reunification.

cases.court: Intermediate Court of Appeals of Hawai'i
cases.holding: The ICA held that HRS § 587A-13 does not require a parent whose rights were already terminated under HRS § 587A-33 to be summoned when a later petition concerning the same child is filed.
cases.quote: We hold that HRS § 587A-13 does not require that a parent whose parental rights have been terminated be summoned if a subsequent petition concerning the child is filed.

relevance.OUT-05: It settles who must be noticed and joined when a child welfare case is reopened after a prior termination, which controls whether a later dismissal or new case binds the former parent.

cases.case_name: Peer News LLC v. City & County of Honolulu
cases.holding: The court held that the Office of Information Practices palpably erred in reading a categorical deliberative process privilege into HRS § 92F-13(3), because that exception requires an individualized showing that disclosure would frustrate a legitimate government function.
cases.quote: OIP palpably erred in adopting a deliberative process privilege pursuant to the HRS § 92F-13(3) exception for documents that would frustrate a legitimate government function if disclosed

relevance.INP-09: Oversight bodies and the public can reach agency deliberative records absent a record-specific frustration showing.
relevance.FAIL-06: An agency cannot withhold internal child-welfare analyses as a class; each withholding needs an individualized justification.
relevance.PMC-02: Audit and budget-related internal records are not categorically exempt from a UIPA request.
relevance.PMC-03: Citizen review work depends on access to the deliberative records this decision opened up.
relevance.PMC-05: This is the leading Hawai'i decision narrowing the exemption most often invoked to defeat public-records requests.
relevance.PMC-06: Systematic cross-analysis of state records is legally feasible because Hawai'i rejects blanket deliberative withholding.

cases.case_name: Honolulu Civil Beat Inc. v. Department of the Attorney General
cases.holding: The court applied the UIPA's presumption of openness in reviewing the Attorney General's refusal to release an investigative report, holding that the agency bears the burden of establishing that a claimed exemption, including one resting on privilege, actually applies.
cases.quote: The UIPA contains a strong presumption in favor of public disclosure of government records.

relevance.INP-09: Records generated by state investigations of agency conduct are presumptively public, which is how oversight findings become actionable.
relevance.FAIL-06: It places the burden on the withholding agency and states the presumption a requester invokes when records are refused.
relevance.PMC-02: Audit and investigative reports prepared for a state agency are presumptively disclosable.
relevance.PMC-03: The presumption of openness supports citizen panels' access to agency records.
relevance.PMC-05: This is the current Hawai'i Supreme Court statement of the UIPA disclosure presumption.
relevance.PMC-06: Public dashboards and cross-state analysis rest on this presumption of access to government records.

cases.case_name: Civil Beat Law Center for the Public Interest, Inc. v. City and County of Honolulu
cases.holding: The court held that the circuit court erred in dismissing the Sunshine Law complaint, ruling that the law permits but does not require a board to close a meeting concerning personnel matters and does not expose members to criminal penalty for meeting in the open.
cases.quote: The Sunshine Law does not require that meetings related to personnel matters be closed to the public

relevance.INP-09: Boards that oversee agencies cannot use personnel confidentiality as a mandatory reason to exclude the public.
relevance.FAIL-06: Routine closure of oversight-body meetings is not compelled by Hawai'i law and is challengeable.
relevance.PMC-03: This is the controlling Hawai'i authority on whether a citizen or review board must deliberate in public.
relevance.PMC-04: A fatality review body cannot treat personnel-related discussion as automatically requiring a closed session.
relevance.PMC-05: It supplies the open-meetings half of Hawai'i's transparency framework alongside the UIPA cases.
relevance.PMC-06: Systemic accountability analysis depends on meetings of oversight boards being open unless closure is affirmatively justified.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment requires a State to support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence before it may sever completely and irrevocably a parent's rights in a natural child.
cases.quote: due process requires that the State support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence

relevance.OUT-02: This is the federal constitutional floor for the burden of proof in every termination of parental rights case, including under HRS § 587A-33.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that an unwed father was entitled as a matter of due process to a hearing on his fitness before his children were taken from him, and that denying him the hearing given other parents also violated equal protection.
cases.quote: We have concluded that all Illinois parents are constitutionally entitled to a hearing on their fitness before their children are removed from their custody.

relevance.INP-12: Emergency custody must be followed promptly by a hearing on the parent's fitness; presumed unfitness is unconstitutional.
relevance.DEC-04: The federal baseline is that removal without an individualized fitness hearing is constitutionally suspect.
relevance.ACT-05: Protective orders affecting custody must rest on individualized findings rather than categorical presumptions about a parent.

cases.case_name: DeShaney v. Winnebago County Department of Social Services
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that the Due Process Clause imposes no general affirmative federal duty on a State to protect a child from private violence, even where caseworkers received and recorded repeated reports of abuse, while noting that States may impose such duties through their own tort law.
cases.quote: As a general matter, then, we conclude that a State's failure to protect an individual against private violence simply does not constitute a violation of the Due Process Clause.

relevance.INP-01: A report alone does not create a federal constitutional duty, which is why Hawai'i's state-law duty under Kaho'ohanohano is the operative one.
relevance.INP-02: Federal § 1983 liability will not follow from an ignored third-party report absent custody or a state-created danger.
relevance.DEC-01: A screen-out decision is generally not actionable under federal due process, though it may be under Hawai'i negligence law.
relevance.OUT-06: It marks the boundary between federal constitutional claims and state tort claims after a child dies following agency contact.
relevance.FAIL-03: Federal performance failures do not by themselves create a constitutional cause of action for an injured child.
relevance.FAIL-04: The Court expressly left States free to impose affirmative protective duties on their agents, which Hawai'i has done.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court rejected the Article I, anticommandeering and recordkeeping challenges to the Indian Child Welfare Act and held the petitioners lacked standing to press the equal protection and nondelegation challenges to its placement preferences, leaving ICWA in force.
cases.quote: Courts must adhere to the placement preferences absent "good cause" to depart from them.

relevance.INP-11: Where a child is an Indian child, ICWA governs the state proceeding from start to finish and its preferences bind Hawai'i courts.
relevance.ACT-04: ICWA's kinship and tribal placement hierarchy controls unless good cause to depart is shown on the record.
relevance.FAIL-03: The opinion confirms that states must implement ICWA's requirements, including the recordkeeping obligation that documents compliance.
relevance.FAIL-05: The Court declined to reach the equal protection challenge to the preferences for lack of standing, leaving them enforceable.
relevance.PMC-01: ICWA compliance and its recordkeeping requirement remain a measurable federal obligation for state agencies.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
cases.holding: Sitting en banc, the court restated that officials must ordinarily obtain judicial authorization before removing a child and may seize a child without a warrant only on reasonable cause to believe the child faces imminent danger of serious bodily injury, though it found the exception satisfied on those facts.
cases.quote: Under the Fourth Amendment, government officials are ordinarily required to obtain prior judicial authorization before removing a child from the custody of her parent.

relevance.INP-12: This is the circuit's en banc statement of the warrant baseline that governs Hawai'i emergency custody practice.
relevance.DEC-04: Any warrantless removal decision must be justified against the imminent-danger exception this opinion defines.
relevance.ACT-05: Protective measures that seize a child require prior judicial authorization unless the narrow exigency exception applies.
relevance.FAIL-02: It is the controlling Ninth Circuit authority against which an unlawful-removal § 1983 claim in Hawai'i is measured.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
cases.holding: The court held that a caseworker was not entitled to qualified immunity for removing children without a court order where the record showed no articulable imminent risk of serious physical injury, and that the availability of time to obtain a warrant is irrelevant when no such risk exists.
cases.quote: The clearly established case law requires articulable, imminent, and serious physical injury or physical abuse to children to justify removing them from their parents' home without a judicial order.

relevance.INP-12: Generalized concern or suspicion is legally insufficient to support warrantless protective custody.
relevance.DEC-04: It states what an emergency removal decision must articulate contemporaneously to survive later review.
relevance.FAIL-02: It is the clearest circuit statement of the elements a plaintiff must negate to establish an unlawful warrantless removal.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
cases.holding: The court affirmed denial of qualified immunity, holding that a social worker and police officer who coerced entry into a home to investigate an anonymous abuse report, interviewed a child and strip-searched another without a warrant or exigency violated clearly established Fourth and Fourteenth Amendment law.
cases.quote: In our circuit, a reasonable official would have known that the law barred this entry.

relevance.INP-06: An anonymous hotline report does not by itself create the exigency needed to enter a home without a warrant.
relevance.INP-08: The court treated the coerced interview and search of children during an investigative home visit as constitutionally regulated conduct.
relevance.INP-10: Escalating from a screened report to an investigative home visit does not suspend the warrant requirement.
relevance.DEC-02: The decision defines the constitutional limits on how an accepted investigation may be conducted in the home.
relevance.FAIL-02: It is the foundational circuit case that a child-welfare investigation is not an exception to ordinary search and seizure law.

cases.case_name: Mann v. County of San Diego
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
cases.holding: The court held that the County violated parents' Fourteenth Amendment rights by subjecting removed children to invasive medical examinations without notifying the parents and without either parental consent or judicial authorization, absent a medical emergency or risk that evidence would dissipate.
cases.quote: the County is required to notify the parents and obtain parental consent (or a court order) in advance of performing the Polinsky medical examinations

relevance.INP-07: Medical examination of a child taken into protective custody is itself a constitutionally regulated act requiring notice and consent or a court order.
relevance.DEC-02: Investigatory and dual-purpose medical exams during an investigation require parental notice and consent or judicial authorization.
relevance.ACT-06: It marks the boundary between genuinely emergent medical care, which may proceed, and investigatory examinations, which may not.
relevance.FAIL-02: Examining a removed child without parental notice or a court order is an independent constitutional violation beyond the removal itself.

cases.case_name: Capp v. County of San Diego
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
cases.holding: The court held that a father stated a viable First Amendment retaliation claim against a social worker who allegedly threatened dependency proceedings because he questioned the allegations and criticized the agency, and that the worker was not entitled to qualified immunity on that claim.
cases.quote: We also conclude, however, that Plaintiffs plead a viable First Amendment retaliation claim, and that Defendants are not entitled to qualified immunity on this claim.

relevance.FAIL-05: This is the circuit authority allowing a parent to sue a caseworker for retaliating against protected criticism of the agency.

cases.case_name: Tamas v. Department of Social & Health Services
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
cases.holding: The court held that foster children have a Fourteenth Amendment liberty interest in supervision and protection from harm by their foster parents, and denied qualified immunity to licensors and social workers who placed and left children with a foster parent despite warning signs.
cases.quote: The Fourteenth Amendment substantive due process clause protects a foster child's liberty interest in social worker supervision and protection from harm inflicted by a foster parent.

relevance.ACT-03: Once the State places a child in foster care it assumes a constitutional duty of supervision and protection.
relevance.OUT-04: That protective duty runs for as long as the youth remains in the State's foster care custody.
relevance.OUT-06: It is the circuit authority for constitutional claims when a child is seriously harmed while in a licensed foster home.
relevance.FAIL-04: Licensing and placement decisions made despite known warning signs can defeat qualified immunity.
relevance.PMC-04: Licensing history and supervision records are the evidentiary core of any review of harm to a child in care.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
cases.holding: The court affirmed denial of absolute and qualified immunity to social workers who failed to give a mother notice of the detention hearing and then told the juvenile court her whereabouts were unknown, holding that giving notice is a mandatory, non-discretionary act and that the right against judicial deception was clearly established.
cases.quote: An individual has a well-established constitutional right to be free from deception in the presentation of evidence during juvenile dependency proceedings.

relevance.DEC-05: Filing a petition and obtaining detention orders requires truthful representations and actual notice to the parent.
relevance.FAIL-02: Removal orders obtained through misstatements to the juvenile court are actionable notwithstanding absolute or qualified immunity.

cases.holding: On a contested foster placement in which the guardian ad litem and DHS disagreed about the child's best interest, the court held that the family court's HRS § 587-71(d) power to enter further orders in the child's best interests extends to ordering DHS not to move the child from her maternal aunt's home and to exercise its licensing discretion as to that home, but that the family court exceeded its authority by ordering DHS to place the child in an unlicensed boarding home and to pay foster board to the unlicensed aunt; it vacated and remanded.
cases.quote: In the event that DHS opts to license Aunt's home, the family court, without more, may order DHS to place Jane in Aunt's licensed boarding home.

relevance.ACT-03: This is the Hawai'i Supreme Court decision on a contested foster placement that the ICA expressly relied on in In the Interest of AS, 130 Haw. 486, holding that vesting foster custody in DHS does not strip the family court of authority over where the child actually lives.
relevance.ACT-04: It marks the precise limit of a kinship placement order: the court may require DHS to keep a child with a relative and to exercise its licensing discretion, but it may not order placement in, or board payments to, an unlicensed relative home.

cases.case_name: In the Interest of the P Children
cases.holding: The court held that an indigent parent's constitutional right to counsel is not invoked for structural-error purposes until the parent appears and engages in the case, including complying with the court's indigency process, affirmed the permanent custody and adoption orders because the years-long proceeding was fundamentally fair, and directed family courts to make an indigency determination at a parent's first appearance.
cases.quote: we direct family courts to make an indigency determination at a parent's first appearance in a chapter 587A proceeding that substantially affects parental rights

relevance.DEC-05: It supplies the operational rule that follows the filing of a chapter 587A petition: the family court must determine indigency at the parent's first appearance, and must appoint counsel whenever indigency is uncertain or the parent resists the inquiry.
relevance.FAIL-01: It is the current outer limit on structural-error vacatur of agency-obtained orders: a parent who absents themself from the case's initial proceedings and neglects the court's appointment process cannot use the resulting gap in representation to undo otherwise fundamentally fair best-interest findings.

cases.case_name: Public First Law Center v. Viola
cases.holding: In an original proceeding arising from the death of foster child Isabella Kalua, the court held that the 'legitimate purpose' standard of HRS § 587A-40 for disclosing confidential Child Protective Act records is not limited to the child's best interests, that a legitimate purpose and 'good cause' under HRS § 578-15 exist to release CPA and connected adoption records where a foster child is missing, has suffered a near fatality, been critically injured, or has died, and it granted the petition and ordered disclosure with redactions protecting the surviving siblings.
cases.quote: We hold that the standard for whether a legitimate purpose exists for disclosure of CPA records is not grounded solely in the best interest of the child standard.

relevance.OUT-06: Where a foster child dies or suffers a near fatality, the confidentiality of the CPA and adoption files yields, and the record of how the agency and courts handled the case becomes publicly obtainable.
relevance.FAIL-06: This is the current Hawai'i authority for compelling disclosure of confidential child-welfare case records, and it rejects the narrower best-interests-only test that had been read into the disclosure statute.
relevance.PMC-02: Financial and programmatic scrutiny of how DHS handled a particular case is possible because the underlying case records are disclosable on a legitimate-purpose showing rather than sealed as a class.
relevance.PMC-04: It makes the raw material of a fatality or near-fatality review — the CPA and adoption case files themselves — obtainable by the public, and the court expressly aligned that result with 42 U.S.C. § 5106a(b)(2)(B)(x).
relevance.PMC-05: It carries Hawai'i's transparency line past the 2018-2020 UIPA decisions and supplies the disclosure route for sealed family court records that the UIPA does not reach.
relevance.PMC-06: Cross-case analysis of Hawai'i child-welfare failures is legally feasible because sealed CPA and adoption records can be unsealed on a legitimate-purpose showing subject to redaction.

cases.holding: The court held that, as an aspect of procedural due process, a parent who needs an interpreter must be provided one at any family court proceeding where parental rights are substantially affected, a question resolved case by case rather than by a bright-line test, but affirmed the award of foster custody to DHS because the mother showed neither a need for an interpreter nor substantial prejudice and DHS proved harm by a preponderance of the evidence.
cases.quote: Procedural due process requires that an individual whose rights are at stake understand the nature of the proceedings he or she faces.

relevance.DEC-03: It confirms that the adjudicatory finding of harm or threatened harm that supports foster custody is made on a preponderance of the evidence, in contrast to the clear and convincing standard that governs termination.
relevance.DEC-05: This is the pre-T.M. authority holding that due process protections attach whenever a family court proceeding substantially affects parental rights, decided case by case with no bright-line test; In re T.M. (2014) later replaced that case-by-case approach for the appointment of counsel.

cases.case_name: In re the Guardianship of Doe
cases.court: Intermediate Court of Appeals of Hawai'i
cases.holding: The ICA held that in deciding whether to terminate or continue a non-parent's guardianship of a minor the family court must consider the parental preference of HRS § 571-46(1) within the best-interests inquiry, adopting for Hawai'i a rebuttable custody presumption in favor of parents, but affirmed continuation of the grandparents' guardianship because the family court implicitly considered that preference and the evidence supported its order.
cases.quote: we believe our jurisdiction is similar to the majority of jurisdictions which adopt a custody presumption in favor of parents subject to rebuttal

relevance.INP-05: This is the origin of the rebuttable parental presumption in Hawai'i guardianship practice that In re Guardianship of I.W. and T.E. later grounded in article I, sections 5 and 6, so a parent who seeks or consents to a guardianship starts from that presumption.
relevance.ACT-04: A kin caregiver seeking guardianship of a child must overcome the statutory preference for the parent, which the family court is required to consider even when the proposed caregivers are grandparents.
relevance.OUT-03: It is the foundational Hawai'i decision treating guardianship as a permanency arrangement and fixing the weight the parental preference carries against a non-parent guardian.

cases.case_name: In re the Guardianship of Doe
cases.court: Intermediate Court of Appeals of Hawai'i
cases.holding: The ICA held that the heightened clear and convincing standard of proof required to terminate parental rights does not apply to the parental-fitness question in a minor guardianship proceeding, because a guardianship of the person of a minor is neither absolute nor irrevocable, and it vacated the denial of the grandparents' co-guardianship petition and remanded for reconsideration.
cases.quote: We conclude the family court erred in applying a heightened standard of proof to the question of the fitness of the natural father.

relevance.INP-05: It held that parental fitness in a guardianship need not be proved by clear and convincing evidence — precisely the rule In re Guardianship of I.W. and T.E. displaced on state constitutional grounds in 2026 — so anyone relying on pre-2026 guardianship authority must check this holding first.
relevance.OUT-03: Anyone researching guardianship permanency in Hawai'i must know that this ICA decision's rejection of the heightened standard for parental fitness no longer states the law after In re Guardianship of I.W. and T.E.

notes: All 35 cases were retrieved from CourtListener in this session and every quote was machine-verified as an exact substring of the retrieved opinion text (whitespace and curly quotes normalized). No unpublished memorandum decisions were used: every Hawai'i decision cited carries a 'FOR PUBLICATION' designation or a bound-reporter citation.

Mandatory reporting: no Hawai'i appellate decision construing HRS § 350-1.1 (persons required to report) or HRS § 350-3 (immunity for good-faith reporters) exists on CourtListener; targeted searches of both haw and hawapp returned zero on-point results. INP-01, INP-02, INP-06, INP-07 and INP-08 therefore rest on Kaho'ohanohano v. DHS (the duty DHS owes once a report is received), In the Interest of Doe, 91 Haw. 166 (threatened harm suffices), and the federal floor. Reporter immunity in Hawai'i remains a matter of unlitigated statute.

ICWA: In the Interest of "A" Children, 119 Haw. 28, holds squarely that ICWA does not reach Native Hawaiian children and applies only where there is an 'Indian child.' Hawai'i has no state ICWA analogue, no state qualified-expert-witness or active-efforts statute, and no reported decision on transfer to tribal court. INP-11 is consequently the thinnest node in the jurisdiction and is served by that ICA holding plus Haaland v. Brackeen. A recent unpublished ICA memorandum, In re Guardianship of E.K. (hawapp, Sept. 4, 2026), mentions ICWA but was not used because it is unpublished and the published 'A' Children holding controls.

Extended foster care: no Hawai'i decision was found construing HRS §§ 346-391 to 346-395 (Young Adult Voluntary Foster Care Program, care to age 21) or HRS § 587A-3.1 (rights of children in foster care, which by its own terms creates no private cause of action). OUT-04 rests on In Interest of Doe, 84 Haw. 41 (reversing foster board payments past the minor's eighteenth birthday on that record), In the Interest of Doe, 96 Haw. 272 (State funding obligation to a ward), and Tamas (duration of the protective duty while in care).

Section 1983 wrongful removal: Hawai'i state courts have produced no published decision on § 1983 liability for removal, so FAIL-02 and DEC-04 are built on Ninth Circuit law, which binds federal courts in Hawai'i. Rogers v. County of San Joaquin, 487 F.3d 1288 (9th Cir. 2007), is the anchor authority and was retrieved and read, but its rule sentence runs 41 words and could not be quoted within the 30-word limit without dropping a condition; Kirkpatrick v. County of Washoe (en banc) states the same warrant baseline in quotable form and is used instead. Keates v. Koile, 883 F.3d 1228, was also retrieved but its rule sentence is broken by a page header in the source text, making an exact-substring quote impossible.

Troxel v. Granville, 530 U.S. 57 (2000), was deliberately excluded: its lead opinion is a four-Justice plurality, not a majority, and the brief's quoting rule requires a majority opinion. The fit-parent presumption enters this layer through In re Guardianship of I.W. and T.E. (Haw. 2026), which adopts and anchors it in article I, sections 5 and 6 of the Hawai'i Constitution.

In re Guardianship of I.W. and T.E. has no reporter citation yet (decided June 16, 2026) and is cited in slip form; the docket number SCWC-23-0000356 was confirmed from the CourtListener docket record because the opinion text on CourtListener redacts docket numbers.

Right to counsel is the most active line of Hawai'i child-welfare law and the five cases in this brief must be read together as a sequence: In the Interest of Doe, 99 Haw. 522 (2002) states the pre-T.M. case-by-case due-process approach; In re T.M. (2014) creates the state constitutional right to appointed counsel; In re L.I. and H.D.K. (2021) moves the attachment point back to the filing of a family supervision petition and makes the failure structural error; In re J.M. and Z.M. (ICA 2021) extends the requirement to the whole proceeding; In re J.H. (2023) holds that a later discharge of counsel is judged for fundamental fairness rather than as automatic structural error; and In the Interest of the P Children (2025) holds that the right is not invoked for structural-error purposes until the parent appears and engages. A practitioner citing T.M. alone will overstate the current rule.

PMC-01 through PMC-06 (CFSR monitoring, OIG/Single Audit, Citizen Review Panels, fatality review commissions, FOIA, and the Project Milk Carton analytic layer) have no Hawai'i case law directly construing CAPTA § 5106a(c) citizen review panels or CFSR obligations. These nodes are mapped to Hawai'i's transparency line (Peer News, Honolulu Civil Beat, Civil Beat Law Center and now Public First Law Center v. Viola) plus Kaho'ohanohano and Tamas for the accountability mechanism that actually operates in this jurisdiction. FAIL-03 is likewise thin: In the Interest of AS, 132 Haw. 368, is the only Hawai'i decision found that construes a Title IV-E requirement, and it rejected the federal-preference theory advanced there; DeShaney supplies the federal boundary.

Missing children from care and sibling-placement preference: no Hawai'i appellate authority was found on either subject. Placement disputes are governed by In the Interest of Doe, 101 Haw. 220 (family court's further-orders power over a contested placement), In the Interest of AS, 132 Haw. 368 (agency discretion, preponderance burden on the challenger) and In the Interest of AS, 130 Haw. 486 (family court must make its own best-interest determination).

Records confidentiality inside a CPA case is governed by In the Interest of RGB, 123 Haw. 1, which upheld limits on a parent's prospective access to the confidential court record, and now by Public First Law Center v. Viola, which governs non-party public access to those same sealed files; public access to agency (non-court) records is governed by the UIPA and Sunshine Law cases. These are distinct regimes and should not be conflated in the FAIL-06 / PMC-05 layer.

Naming caution for anyone re-checking these citations: Hawai'i anonymized child-protective appeals are styled 'In the Interest of Doe' or 'In re Doe' across many different cases and decades. Seven distinct 'Doe' decisions appear here (84 Haw. 41; 91 Haw. 166; 95 Haw. 183; 96 Haw. 272; 99 Haw. 522; 100 Haw. 335; 101 Haw. 220; 108 Haw. 144), plus two 'In re the Guardianship of Doe' decisions (93 Haw. 374; 106 Haw. 75), and two distinct cases are styled 'In the Interest of AS' (132 Haw. 368, Supreme Court 2014; 130 Haw. 486, ICA 2013). The cluster_id is the reliable identifier.

The pre-existing layers.case_law.key_cases entries in the HI node files are keyword-matched noise (COVID-19 judiciary orders, tax appeals, arbitration, hospice licensing, adult conservatorships). Every title was treated only as a candidate name; none survived retrieval and none is retained in this brief.

Two Ninth Circuit opinions in this set (Mann, Rieman, Capp, Demaree, Kirkpatrick) carry a court-staff 'SUMMARY' block that expressly states it is no part of the opinion. All quotes used here were positionally verified to fall in the opinion body, after that block. SCOTUS quotes were positionally verified to fall within the majority opinion and before any concurrence or dissent.

Added In the Interest of Doe, 101 Haw. 220, 65 P.3d 167 (2003) (cluster 2625940) for ACT-03, ACT-04: retrieved and read in this session; it is the 'March 2003 Doe' the ICA expressly relied on in In the Interest of AS, 130 Haw. 486 ('March 2003 Doe supports our holding'), and that reliance was verified by retrieving and reading the AS ICA opinion text (opinion 6493633), which cites it as In re Doe, 101 Hawai'i 220, 231, 65 P.3d 167, 178 (2003). Note for anyone re-checking: the CourtListener cluster carries date_filed 2003-04-22 (the amended opinion) even though the ICA's shorthand refers to it as the March 2003 decision. The placement layer previously cited both AS decisions without the supreme court case they are built on.

Added In the Interest of the P Children, No. SCWC-22-0000636 (Haw. Feb. 13, 2025) (cluster 10332851) for DEC-05, FAIL-01: retrieved and read; published ('FOR PUBLICATION'), with a separate dissent by Devens, J. at cluster 10332762 that was not quoted. The prior brief omitted it only because the cluster carries no reporter citation and the docket number is redacted in the opinion text; that rationale is inconsistent with the brief's own slip-form treatment of In re Guardianship of I.W. and T.E., so the same fix was applied — the docket number SCWC-22-0000636 was confirmed from the CourtListener docket record (docket 68072315). It is the current limit on the L.I./T.M. structural-error rule.

Added Public First Law Center v. Viola, No. SCPW-24-0000464 (Haw. Sept. 30, 2025) (cluster 10682020) for OUT-06, FAIL-06, PMC-02, PMC-04, PMC-05, PMC-06: retrieved and read; published, unanimous, no reporter citation yet, docket number SCPW-24-0000464 confirmed from the CourtListener docket record (docket 71502830). It arises from the death of foster child Isabella Kalua and is the decision that lets the public reach sealed CPA and adoption case files where a foster child is missing, critically injured or dead. Its addition cures the currency problem flagged by the verifier: the transparency layer no longer rests entirely on 2018-2020 authority. It also supersedes the narrower reading of 'legitimate purpose' drawn from Kema, 91 Haw. 200.

Added In the Interest of Doe, 99 Haw. 522, 57 P.3d 447 (2002) (cluster 2602460) for DEC-03, DEC-05: retrieved and read; this is the decision In re T.M. cites at 99 Hawai'i at 533, 57 P.3d at 459. Practitioners should note what it actually holds — it is an interpreter/language-access and due-process case establishing that protections attach wherever parental rights are 'substantially affected,' resolved case by case with no bright-line test — and that T.M. superseded that case-by-case approach for appointment of counsel specifically. It was not mapped to OUT-02 only because that node is already at the six-case cap.

Added In re the Guardianship of Doe, 93 Haw. 374, 4 P.3d 508 (Haw. Ct. App. 2000) (cluster 2595363) for INP-05, ACT-04, OUT-03: retrieved and read; published. It is the origin of Hawai'i's rebuttable parental-custody presumption in guardianship proceedings, which In re Guardianship of I.W. and T.E. (2026) later elevated to a state constitutional requirement of clear and convincing evidence of unfitness.

Added In re the Guardianship of Doe, 106 Haw. 75, 101 P.3d 684 (Haw. Ct. App. 2004) (cluster 6614269) for INP-05, OUT-03: retrieved and read; published. It held that the clear and convincing standard governing termination does not apply to the parental-fitness question in a minor guardianship because a guardianship is 'neither absolute nor irrevocable' — precisely the holding I.W. and T.E. displaced on constitutional grounds. Caution: the opinion rejects the heightened standard and points to the general preponderance rule of HRS § 571-41(c) only by comparison; it contains no express statement adopting preponderance for fitness, so it should be described as rejecting clear-and-convincing rather than as adopting preponderance.

Node-map repair: INP-03, INP-04, INP-08 and DEC-06 each carried only one cluster_id in the prior node_map even though verified case entries already contained node-specific relevance sentences for them. Those mappings were restored, not invented — INP-03 now also lists Kaho'ohanohano (Maui Police Department report to DHS) and In the Interest of Doe, 91 Haw. 166 (DHS disclosure to police); INP-04 now also lists In re AA (Rule 24 intervention by a parent who surfaces after the case opens) and 91 Haw. 166 (verified-petition mechanics); INP-08 now also lists 91 Haw. 166 (one child's disclosure supporting a petition as to a sibling) and Calabretta (constitutional limits on interviewing children during an investigation); DEC-06 now also lists In re L.I. and H.D.K. (right to counsel attaches on a family supervision petition) and 91 Haw. 166 (family supervision on a threatened-harm showing without removal). Several other nodes were likewise reconciled with relevance sentences already present in verified entries. After this pass every one of the 42 nodes carries between 2 and 6 cases.

No additional published Hawai'i authority exists for INP-03 or INP-08 beyond what is mapped. Targeted searches in this session for HRS § 587A-8 (police protective custody) returned only In re J.H. as published — In Re: P.L., 153 Haw. 432 (ICA 2024), In re: The Guardianship of KK, 153 Haw. 231 (ICA 2023) and In re: LC, AC, IC, and DG, 150 Haw. 155 (ICA 2021) are all expressly 'NOT FOR PUBLICATION.' A search for 'mandated reporter' in haw and hawapp returned a single hit, AB v. MF, 151 Haw. 353 (ICA 2022), which is also not for publication. Educator and law-enforcement reporting duties in Hawai'i therefore remain served by the state duty case (Kaho'ohanohano), the threatened-harm petition case (91 Haw. 166), In re J.H. for police protective custody, and the federal Fourth Amendment standard of Calabretta v. Floyd.

Every authority the verifier named as missing was located, retrieved and read in this session, and all six were real and on point; there is no authority in that list that could not be verified. The only judgment calls made were (a) not mapping In the Interest of the P Children or In the Interest of Doe, 99 Haw. 522 to OUT-02, which is already at the six-case cap and adequately covered, and (b) not mapping In the Interest of Doe, 101 Haw. 220 to OUT-03, because its holding concerns foster placement and licensing rather than a permanency outcome.

Missing (for a later pass): Lassiter v. Department of Social Services, 452 U.S. 18 (1981) — the federal benchmark for appointed counsel in termination proceedings, holding due process requires counsel only on a case-by-case basis. The brief builds an entire six-case Hawai'i right-to-counsel sequence (T.M., L.I. and H.D.K., J.M. and Z.M., J.H., P Children, 99 Haw. 522) without the decision those cases are consciously departing from; In re T.M. grounds the categorical right in article I, section 5 of the Hawai'i Constitution precisely because Lassiter declined to do so federally. Its absence makes the Hawai'i rule look unremarkable when its significance is that it is broader than the federal floor.

Missing (for a later pass): Kema v. Gaddis, 91 Haw. 200, 982 P.2d 334 (1999) — the Hawai'i Supreme Court's prior decision on disclosure of confidential CPA records, and the case Public First Law Center v. Viola expressly overrules 'as to its narrow interpretation of "legitimate purpose"' (confirmed in the Viola opinion text). The brief mentions it only in a trailing note. Any practitioner researching CPA record access will hit Kema first, and a brief that omits it entirely gives no warning that the leading prior authority is now partly overruled. It belongs in FAIL-06 / PMC-05 with an explicit superseded flag, exactly as 106 Haw. 75 is flagged in OUT-03.

Missing (for a later pass): Honolulu Civil Beat Inc. v. Department of the Attorney General, 151 Haw. 74, 508 P.3d 1160 (2022) — a later and distinct UIPA decision from the 2020 case (146 Haw. 285) already in the brief, holding that where only part of a record is exempt the record may be withheld entirely only if permissible redactions are so extensive that what remains is misleading (quoted and applied in Viola, which reversed a family court that had relied on exactly that misleading-redaction rationale). This is the controlling redaction rule for the FAIL-06 / PMC-05 layer and the most current UIPA statement; its omission leaves the brief citing the 2020 decision as if it were the last word.

Missing (for a later pass): In re Interest of FG, 142 Haw. 497, 421 P.3d 1267 (2018) — the Hawai'i Supreme Court decision on confidentiality of chapter 587A records and the CAPTA state-plan confidentiality conditions (relied on in Viola for the 42 U.S.C. 5106a(b)(1)(A) and (b)(2)(B)(viii) framework). It is the Hawai'i authority tying CPA confidentiality to federal funding conditions and is the natural bridge between the FAIL-06 records layer and the PMC-01/PMC-03 federal-compliance nodes, which the brief concedes are its thinnest.

Missing (for a later pass): In re Guardianship of John Doe, 7 Haw. App. 575, 786 P.2d 519 (1990) — the earlier ICA decision that a non-parent cannot prevail over a parent in a custody contest absent a valid finding of unfitness or an unstable home (quoted as the governing rule in In re the Guardianship of Doe, 106 Haw. 75, which is in the brief). It is the root of the Hawai'i parental-fitness line the brief traces from 93 Haw. 374 through 106 Haw. 75 to I.W. and T.E.; INP-05 and OUT-03 are incomplete without it.

Missing (for a later pass): Troxel v. Granville, 530 U.S. 57 (2000) — the fit-parent presumption the Hawai'i Supreme Court adopted and constitutionalized in In re Guardianship of I.W. and T.E. The brief's stated reason for excluding it (plurality, so no majority to quote) is a defensible application of its own quoting rule, but declining to quote an authority is a different decision from excluding it entirely. Any opposing brief will cite Troxel, and a practitioner reading OUT-03 and ACT-01 should see where the presumption comes from even if the entry carries a holding summary in place of a quotation.
